If we continue to pollute our atmosphere, the local effects of climate change are likely to be severe.We have now had three years in a decade (2005, 2010 and 2014) when we have broken the record for global average temperatures. 2014 was the hottest year globally. His term might be extended for a few years, it might not. Windy Wellington is not usually a greatly fought-for posting among the political class. headline: Open streaming an Olympic precursor
intro: The technology chief of the joint venture between Seven West Media and technology giant Yahoo! has said its move into multi-channel, multiplatform live broadcasting during this year’s Australian Open tennis tournament will pave the way for future on demand live sports coverage. In a bid to catch the viewing attention of fans who get so involved they don’t want to miss a minute, Yahoo!7 has begun serving up matches on all 16 courts at this year’s Australian Open, live-streamed to PC, laptop, tablet or smartphones. It is a move the company said had been a success with viewers, and which could be replicated for other events such as the Olympic Games. Yahoo!7 chief technology officer Craig Penfold said this year’s project brief was clear. ‘‘To provide the best, most comprehensive tennis experience we can to users; giving the users the ability to choose what they want to watch,’’ he said. The platform features two ‘‘megawalls’’ modelled on the TV version, but viewers can click on their chosen court. The service is free, with the company developing an embedded code that responds to ‘‘cues’’ in a match, such as a drinks break, for when an advertising spot can be played.Mr Penfold said this innovation was the answer to the conundrum of inserting advertising in sports coverage with no clearly defined break times. ‘‘When you go into the live streams, it is the raw stream coming out of the broadcast compound.What we needed to do was introduce technology into the live streams, which has never been done before by Yahoo!,’’ he said. The next challenge after generating some income for the platform was to find a way to stream 16 courts without ‘‘breaking the internet’’. The platform has ample bandwidth to support even the most gripping of five-setters, Mr Penfold said. ‘‘The capacity at the moment is going quite well, we’ve seen a lot of enthusiasm from our users.’’ Data collected within the first few days of the Open showed more than 1 million streams, and 3.7 million minutes of the Open, and 45 per cent of streaming was on tablet, meaning people were either dual-screening while watching another match or channel on TV, or watching the tennis on the go. Testing the platform through the earlier tournaments, including the Hopman Cup and the Brisbane International, allowed the engineers to tweak and improve the user experience. It also relied on feedback from the app stores. ‘‘The really great thing about apps and app stores is you get really immediate feedback from people, we can see from our users what they really want to be doing,’’ Mr Penfold said. ‘‘It is one of the most innovative and exciting projects I’ve had to work on, it’s been great to see user feedback. It is really gratifying for my team in particular how we can delight our users.’’ The tennis is just the beginning, Mr Penfold said, with opportunities in the next few years to expand the service, including the Rio de Janeiro Olympic Games and the Commonwealth Games on the Gold Coast. The live-streaming option changes the traditional power dynamic in broadcasting, giving viewers, rather than programmers, control of what to watch. This means criticism of past major sporting events coverage, such as an over-emphasis on swimming in Olympic Games, and a lack of coverage of sports in which Australians aren’t competing, would be negated. Yahoo!7’s offering is no small project for the company either. Mr Penfold said it had required up to 40 people, with teams in Melbourne and Sydney to ensure it would work. Mr Penfold, however, declined to disclose the amount of money the company had to invest to provide the service. ‘‘It is appropriate in size to the strategic value and the innovation.’’

In a news release, the NYSE described bitcoin as ‘‘an important growth market’’ and hoped its involvement would ‘‘bring additional transparency’’ to the bitcoin market’s pricing. But the price of bitcoin is looking miserable. In January its value has fallen 44 per cent; the price plunged through its $US200 resistance point and reached a low of $US177. In a bid to explain the fall, some analysts have pointed to the hack of popular exchange Bitstamp and the loss of $US5 million worth of bitcoin, suggesting it has shaken confidence, despite Bitstamp being back up and running within a few days. Ever regulation-antsy, bitcoin markets may also be spooked by the continuation of the Silk Road trial, which began in New York City last week. Ross Ulbricht, 30, is accused of being the mastermind, known as Dread Pirates Robots, behind the online global black market website, which sold more than $US200 million worth of drugs to customers using the anonymous bitcoin as payment. He has pleaded not guilty to charges, including attempting to arrange six murders, money laundering, computer hacking and conspiracy to traffic narcotics. United States government prosecutors allege Ulbricht took a cut of almost $US18 million in bitcoin between January 2011 and October 2013, through drug deals of heroin, cocaine and crystal meth via the website. He faces life in prison if convicted. Regulations are likely to spring out of the Silk Road case, which has the decentralised currency markets worried. However, there are fast-moving players in venture capital rushing to back new bitcoin businesses springing up the world over. CoinDesk data released this month showed the amount of venture capital ploughed into bitcoin start-ups in 2014 was more than three times that of 2013. They raised $US314.7 million in total, compared with $US938 million in 2013.

headline: Australia launches cyber weapons
intro: The frequency and severity of global cyber attacks is rising rapidly and extending into outright cyber war between states. And Australia is no innocent bystander, developing its own cyber weapons, which we can reveal for the first time have been deployed in counterterrorist operations overseas. On June 27 North Korea’s Ambassador to the United Nations, Ja Song-nam, sent a letter to UN Secretary-GeneralBan Ki-moon, warning that if the US allowed Sony Pictures Entertainment to release a comedy, called The Interview, on a CIA plot to assassinate North Korean dictator Kim Jong-un, it would be tantamount to ‘‘undisguised sponsoring of terrorism as well as an act of war’’. After infiltrating Sony’s computer network for months and stealing over 100 terabytes of confidential data (including the next James Bond movie script) on November 24, a North Korean hacking collective called the ‘‘Guardians of Peace’’ (aka ‘‘GOP’’) leaked three unreleased Sony films, sensitive salary details and embarrassing email correspondence between top executives and actors. They also installed the immensely destructive ‘‘Wiper’’malware on numerous Sony computers, which erased information, rendered the machines inoperable, and shut down the entire Sony network for more than six weeks. On 18 and 19 December the hackers demanded Sony cancel the December 25 premiere of The Interview and threatened physical attacks on any venues that aired it. Sony promptly withdrew the film. The FBI says the malware was compiled on Korean-language computers and is similar to the code that was used in a 2013 North Korean cyber attack on South Korea’s banking system. The US response was swift. Convinced by evidence garnered from the NSA’s penetration of North Korea’s networks, President Barack Obama, a former civil rights lawyer, sensationally declared on December 19 that the US would retaliate ‘‘proportionally’’ and ‘‘in a place and time and manner that we choose’’.The characteristically cautious Obama had no doubt about the source of the attacks or the need to react decisively, The New York Times reported. US Cyber Command did not wait long. On December 23, and again on December 28, North Korea’s internet and wireless networks were wiped out. ‘‘At Pyongyang time 7:30pm [on December 28], North Korea’s internet and mobile 3G network came to a standstill,’’ Chinese state media said. In early January Obama also signed off on additional sanctions for North Korea’s ‘‘destructive, coercive cyber related actions during November and December 2014’’,which ‘‘constitute a continuing threat to the national security, foreign policy and economy of the United States’’. North Korea’s brazen attack highlights how the cyber domain is increasingly chaotic and hazardous despite sustained efforts to establish security mitigants. It also sets a worrying precedent for autocracies fearful of rebuke. Edward Snowden’s patron, Russia, is probably a pioneer. In November it was fingered by Mandiant for sponsoring hacks on major financial institutions, which have exposed tens of millions households, in response to Western sanctions following its invasion of the Ukraine. Russian Foreign Ministry spokesman Alexander Lukashevich has leapt to North Korea’s defence over Sony, claiming that ‘‘the concept of the movie [The Interview] is so aggressive and scandalous that the reaction of the North Korean side ... is quite understandable’’. ‘‘We perceive US threats to take revenge ... as absolutely counterproductive and dangerous, as they only would add tensions to the already difficult situation on the Korean Peninsula and could lead to further escalation of conflict,’’Mr Lukashevich said. On January 8Wiredreported that ‘‘amid all the noise the Sony hack generated ... a far more troubling cyber attack was largely lost in the chaos’’. Germany’s Federal Office for that ‘‘advanced’’ hackers had broken into and physically destroyed part of a German steel mill by ‘‘manipulating and disrupting control systems to such a degree that a blast furnace could not be properly shut down’’,which caused ‘‘massive damage to the system’’. Australia is no passive participant in these cyber conflicts. Multiple intelligence sources have told The Australian Financial Review that for more than a decade we have been building an offensive ‘‘computer network attack’’ (CNA) capability inside the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD),which openly advertises for hackers who are ‘‘passionate about breaking and securing computer systems’’with ‘‘knowledge of offensive and defensive techniques to protect Australia’s interests’’. Sources say ASD has launched cyber attacks on terrorists in the Middle East that were conspiring against Australia. ASD’s small team of CNA specialists,which are a fraction of the people working in its ‘‘computer network exploitation’’ area (which steals foreign intelligence), develop their own malware and borrow payloads from the larger CNA resources residing inside America’s NSA and Britain’s GCHQ. Australia has also allegedly harnessed its offensive cyber skills to hit back against a non-democratic state that was pilfering our public and private secrets, intelligence sources say.This involved implanting malware on foreign servers that erased data and disabled the cooling systems such that they were ultimately ‘‘fried’’. Every day we seem to learn of new black swans lurking in cyberspace, which reinforce the need for governments, companies and individuals to pre-emptively protect themselves. So despite the revelations of fugitive former NSA contractor Edward Snowden (who has notably never leaked NSA information on the privacy and civil rights abuses of Russia and China’s security agencies), the US, UK and many European nations continue to support mandatory data retention policies. The issue with the metadata debate is that the cost-benefit analysis lacks balance. Journalists have done a great job explaining the low probability risk of a democratic government systematically exploiting metadata to the detriment of its own electorate. In this context, calls for more oversight and controls when people access data are spot-on. There has, however, been less time committed to understanding the ever changing threat landscape. Many of those who rail against metadata retention are the same ‘‘anarcho libertarians’’who dismiss the tsunami of evidence that the internet is being hijacked by individuals and state and non-state entities that want to undermine our way of life.

headline: Port claim nonsense

headline: Audit more than camps

headline: France shows the West at its best
intro: The jihadist killers of 17 people in France have failed. Instead of intimidation and division, their assault on journalists, police officers, and French Jews has had the stunning and quite unexpected effect of reminding Western democracies of who they are, and what they stand for. Four million people in France marched last weekend to support the existence of a magazine they hardly read, probably wouldn't like if they did, and show staunch resistance to those who would shut it by force. It was a spontaneous, instinctive demonstration of the power of secular, pluralist society, echoed around the world. France's pluralism made this a great civic revolt against terror, not Muslims; it included them and commemorated their victims too. Democracy and pluralism has to be much bigger than those who hold it in contempt. That is what we saw in Paris last Sunday.

As societies and attitudes change, utterances that were commonplace only a decade ago are less acceptable now, even amid the generalised coarsening of much common culture. But left progressives and others have gone further by seeking to impose various forms of censorship against views with which they disagree. They have used social media assaults, such as the online petition against Myer chief executive Bernie Brookes by the Australian Human Rights Disability Commissioner for reasonably pointing out that raising taxes to finance higher public spending on disability care would come from the pockets of his customers. headline: True liberty does not require causing offence
intro: The reporting and commentary on the Charlie Hebdo terrorist strike places focus on the human right of freedom of speech. Our tradition of free speech links it to responsibility of its use, with an application of prudence as for its consequences. Prudence is an oft forgotten virtue; its application ought to always precede the deeds of fortitude. In what is a clash of cultures, nothing is gained through deliberate offence. True liberty does not require it. It is well documented that Charlie Hebdo took pride in its "fortitude", as well as a broader delight in disparaging all things religious of all faiths. From a Christian view, in doing so they lack charity.

headline: Temporary visas make good business sense
intro: The Abbott government is picking a fight with unions and professional groups in its plan to overhaul the visa system, including a new category of year-long, "short-term mobility" temporary work visas. But it is a fight worth having. Attempts by Labor, the Greens and some minority senators to block changes that would make the visa system more flexible and permit companies to hire specialised workers wherever they can find them, are little more than populism. The new visa category is so far just a proposal, as part of a review of the skilled immigration system announced in October. It recognises the long-standing reality of the labour market - that there are comparatively small numbers of specialised, highly paid workers who can and will move between countries as their skills are required. The same goes for many white-collar and white-coated professions. Many thousands of Australians work overseas in specialised categories and they too are a world away from the mass of the workers the traditional labour movement thinks it is defending. Businesses need the flexibility to bring in such workers for whatever period is required, if some projects are to be made to work. The government worked around a Senate disallowal of new visa categories for offshore workers in July by using its regulatory powers, but that was a temporary measure. It is to be hoped that when the proposed changes in visa categories are presented to the Senate, that body will finally acknowledge the reality of a labour market of specialised skills. By blocking new types of visas, and killing projects before they start, they will be harming the prospects of many workers rather than protecting them.

headline: Plus and minus in the oil price

It's the biggest drop since the global financial crisis in 2008. But the causes this time around are more complicated. In the powerhouse of China, economic growth is de-linking from raw materials as the economy turns away from flat-out construction and towards consumption. In oil, there is a price war among suppliers, as Saudi Arabia plays a bigger and more aggressive version of the same game Rio Tinto and BHP Billiton have been playing in iron ore: using the downturn to reassert its position as the dominating low-cost supplier. Australian energy is not so well placed. Our newer and sometimes excessively expensive LNG projects may now face a wave of painful asset write-downs as cheaper oil flows through into lower export gas prices over the next few months.

The Coalition did not obtain a plurality of support in the last election that our constitution requires for them to be able to solely pass legislation through both houses. Why are the crossbenchers singled out, but Labor's senate opposition is winked at? We should be cautious about removing checks and balances, and should not be doing so on the basis of persons speaking on behalf of (non-voting) entities who have a financial interest in supporting the Coalition's supposedly pro-business agenda. It's a very short-sighted exercise by these CEOs. They'd be singing a different tune were it a Labor government's reforms. Yet if we are to be truly independent, we should be regarded as a foreign state, even within the Commonwealth of Nations. Anyone for an honorary KBE? I have no issue with our own knighthoods. intro: Thursday's capex data is just a horrible set of numbers. And if the Reserve Bank of Australia was hoping companies would start taking risks to breathe some life back into the economy, then it would have been very disappointed with the latest outlook for investment spending .

headline: Profit taking, weak data crimps ASX rally
intro: Investor's hopes for a push by stocks through the 6000 mark were quashed on Thursday as profit taking ended the market's three-day winning streak, despite several strong earnings results and growing expectations of a March cash rate cut.

headline: Fundies feast on franks
intro: Aside from floats and block trades, equity capital markets bankers have also been keeping themselves busy pitching deals designed to release franking credits.

headline: CIMB research analysts finish up as bank maps retreat
intro: It's the end of an era for equity capital markets on Friday, with CIMB's equity research analysts set to pack up their desks and bid farewell to fund manager clients.

headline: Griffin Coal, Corrs and the $150m court case
intro: The saga engulfing Griffin Coal has taken a fresh twist, with bondholders and receivers sweating over a looming court decision that could render invalid the last payment - of $150 million - due on the sale of the business four years ago to India's Lanco.

headline: Perennial to tap into retail investor search for yield
intro: Perennial Investment Partners is set to cash in on investor appetite for listed investment companies, launching a new fund and equity raising as early as next week.

headline: Greenstone to hit the road ahead of $1.5b float
intro: As bankers try to convince the likes of Youi and Bupa to pursue an ASX listing, Hollard Group's Greenstone is readying for what will likely be one of the biggest insurance floats of the year.

headline: Boomers will keep Ramsay's hospital beds full
intro: Ramsay Health Care chief executive Chris Rex says he can safely spend hundreds of millions each year expanding the group's Australian hospitals because demographic trends almost guarantee the extra beds and operating theatres will be filled.

headline: Masters hives off land
intro: Woolworths' loss-making home improvement chain Masters is carving up car parks and leasing sites to other retailers in an attempt to boost returns on its $2.9 billion investment with joint-venture partner Lowe's.

headline: Slipper fraud quashed
intro: Former parliamentary speaker Peter Slipper has won an ACT Supreme Court appeal against several convictions for defrauding the Commonwealth.

headline: Lyons to quit ACTU after loss
intro: It's said that political processes are like comedy - all about people skills and timing. And it turns out mine are a bit shit. Tim Lyons, on Twitter

headline: Abbott: labelling red tape 'business friendly'
intro: Changing labelling laws for food made in Australia but not for imported products could price locals out of the market despite Prime Minister Tony Abbott's promise that any extra red tape will be "business friendly", a food industry body says.

headline: A phew moment for Joyce
intro: The look on Alan Joyce's face said it all.

headline: National carrier's high here to stay
intro: Qantas Airways expects to bank a $500 million oil bonus over the balance of its financial year as the airline fully exercises the unexpected benefits flowing from OPEC's war on US onshore oil producers.

headline: Take out insurance
intro: It is time for individuals to take more responsibility for their own potential misfortunes. How many of those, or their dependants, who are on disability support had income protection, total and permanent disablement, trauma cover and life insurance? There is such an embedded mentality of entitlement that has to be addressed.

headline: Triggs mishandled
intro: Following Prime Minister Tony Abbott's unhelpful linking of past aid to Indonesia to the death row appeal of two convicted drug traffickers, Abbott's near rabid verbal attacks on Human Rights Commission president Gillian Triggs are arguably yet another 'captain's call' that has gone awry.

headline: Perpetual's journey out of crisis
intro: Perpetual chief executive Geoff Lloyd deserves to join the elite ranks of business leaders who have guided a top 150 company out of a crisis situation with sub-optimal earnings and low staff morale to the sweet spot of operational success.

headline: Crashing out of the euro
intro: Based on the experience of the past 10 years, it is hard to predict the future of the euro. But Greece looks likely to be the catalyst for trauma. The European Central Bank has no experience here. Brussels has been busy bringing countries into the euro, not managing orderly exits. This week, a deal was done with Greece's ruling Syriza that, in effect, was a major backdown from what that party had promised its constituents. Once the Greeks realise this, they are unlikely to be resigned to accepting the new terms of constraint meekly. Should Greece crash out, the eurozone concept itself will be threatened. Europe is a wonderful continent with a diversity of culture. But the tensions that result from trying to force those differing cultures to operate under a single currency have been strained to the point of breaking.

headline: Holidays part of our tradition
intro: Ramani Venkatramani proposes a radical move to (apparently) overcome the call to extend penalty rates ("Take religion out of our holidays", AFR, February 26). Why stop there? If as a Christian I would be denied a public holiday for Christmas, Good Friday and Easter Monday, then what about those other "religious zealots" who have no problem taking a public holiday for Melbourne Cup Day (not to forget Devonport, Launceston, Adelaide), butchers, bakers, candlestick makers' picnic day, a few Labour days and the birthday of the monarch. There are many bigger issues facing this nation.

headline: Abbott must step aside
intro: It is obvious that the crisis affecting the leadership of the government is continuing. ("How do you think that went, Prime Minister", AFR, February 26). Nothing seems to be going particularly well for the PM right now. MPs in marginal seats are clearly concerned about the handling of various issues including submarines, the Human Rights Commission chair, the letter of the Liberal Party Treasurer, and the imposition of the fee on the purchase of property by foreigners.

headline: Flexibility the key in modern office
intro: It was very disappointing to read Brett Kelly's views around flexible work practices in the accounting industry ("Client satisfaction a full-time business", AFR, March 25). I hope the article was not read as a proxy for how other professional services firms view this matter. In an increasingly mobile world where employees can work from anywhere, any time, a paradigm that says optimal employees are those that are physically in the office from 7am-7pm, five days per week, is both outdated and narrow-minded. Employers who want to work with the most talented individuals recognise that flexibility is key to both attracting and retaining talent.

headline: Let's debate enterprise bargaining
intro: Michael Angwin's criticism of the Abbott government's IR inquiry ("Ill-conceived IR inquiry is doomed from the outset", AFR, February 25) makes a number of telling points about IR research. However, some of them, we believe, are misdirected. To begin with a mild empirical corrective, he states that since 1990 the Journal of Industrial Relations has published only four pieces on enterprise bargaining. On our count it is more like a dozen discrete studies plus about 30 articles in annual reviews of Australian IR that focus on employer and union engagement with enterprise bargaining.

headline: Name and shame the bullies
intro: Tony Abbott says the HRC report on children in detention is "a transparent stitch-up" ("Bribe, inducement, it's still whiffy", AFR, February 25).

headline: Response to oil may set off roller coaster
intro: The axe taken to spending across the oil and gas sector on slumping prices has caused some to question whether we're setting the scene for a spike to $US200 a barrel oil prices as a result.

headline: iSelect profits from diversification
intro: The chief executive of comparison website iSelect, Alex Stevens, says diversifying beyond the company's traditional market of health insurance has allowed the company to move to sustainable growth.

headline: Nine profit takes hit as $150m buyback launched
intro: Nine Entertainment Co chief executive David Gyngell expects the company's regional affiliate WIN Corp to pay more in affiliate fees to reflect rising television production costs, and says he is open to negotiate with WIN's rival Southern Cross Media, as the deal's expiry date looms.

headline: Transfield bid rejection queried
intro: Transfield Services' board will be held accountable for its decision to reject a $1 billion takeover offer from Spanish infrastructure group Ferrovial after the contractor delivered weak first half results, its top investors have warned.

headline: Packer's Vegas relief
intro: The legal saga related to James Packer's failed Las Vegas casino investment from six years ago has ended, with hedge fund financiers winning a settlement of more than $100 million over the bankruptcy.

headline: Backdown on RET position
intro: The government will drop its attempts to make changes to the Renewable Energy Target if the industry rejects its latest offer for a compromise deal, Industry minister Ian Macfarlane has said.

headline: AER's Conboy set for tussle
intro: If the NSW government is thinking of a court challenge in its $8 billion regulatory battle over electricity prices, Paula Conboy has a simple message: "I have never lost a case."

headline: Rank and file is fed up with Liberal Party backstabbing
intro: It would be a mistake for the party to ignore those within who are angry at being taken for granted and who seek transparency.

headline: Abbott finds a week really is a long time in politics
intro: Canberra observed With the drums beating loudly on Tony Abbott's leadership, Monday's security statement seems so long ago.

headline: Top lawyers call for childcare tax breaks
intro: Leading corporate lawyers have called for tax deductibility for childcare and nanny costs following the stark absence of support for it in the Productivity Commission's landmark review on childcare.

headline: Attorney-General is 'just a working person'
intro: Queensland Attorney-General Yvette D'Ath took 14 years to achieve her goal of becoming a lawyer, trudging through night school, working full- time, raising two children.

headline: Inquiry a boon for Minters
intro: Minter Ellison has received almost $8 million for its work for the federal government on the inquiry into trade union corruption. The royal commission was extended to run until December 2015, and will cost taxpayers $50.4 million.

headline: Retired lawyer lured back by virtual practice
intro: When mergers and acquisitions lawyer John Malon retired, in accordance with his top-tier firm's retirement plan, he never envisaged returning to the industry.

headline: Law graduates undeterred by dire job hopes
intro: Nick Symons is well aware of his luck. He got a full-time job as a junior solicitor at personal injuries firm Maliganis Edwards Johnson in Canberra, before he had even finished university in 2013.

headline: Court sheds light on FWC union bias
intro: A judgment by the full Federal Court which excludes unions from negotiating greenfields agreements is most welcome, as it injects some common sense into industrial relations and casts extra light on the Fair Work Commission's adjudication process - light the commission would find uncomfortable.

headline: Wrong lessons on bank failure
intro: David Murray's inquiry assumes that only banks act irrationally, not the people who regulate them. In fact, there are plenty of perverse incentives for the rule-makers too.

headline: Property taxes and global forces
intro: Foreign buyers of a pad in Australia are now going to have to pay more the privilege, with hefty new fees to get their foreign investment approval. The real estate industry is furious at the change, claiming it sends the wrong message to the foreign investors who helped drive a record $54 billion in housing and apartment construction in 2014.

headline: Vocation class action backed
intro: Listed litigation funder IMF Bentham advised the market on Thursday it was backing one of three slated class actions against education company Vocation. Happy news for Vocation's temporary chief financial officer Stewart Cummins, who will present a gruesome half-year result on Monday morning. The share price is clinging to double figures, closing on Thursday at 10.5¢.

headline: Lobbyist fights lobbying
intro: He was once Australia's top bureaucrat, Qantas CEO and an executive at News Corp, but now John Menadue is campaigning against the scourge of evil corporate lobbyists. Plugging his new book on "the public interest" to The Canberra Times, Menadue has bemoaned "what the Minerals Council of Australia did to subvert public discussion" on the mining tax, "the activities of Clubs Australia to thwart gaming reforms" and how "the hotel lobby … effectively determines hotel operating hours".

headline: Qantas out of the clouds
intro: A year ago, the ailing national carrier was struggling with headwinds of competition, oil prices and industrial action. Now it's back in the black. There are several reasons for this dramatic reversal, writes Jamie Freed.

headline: Breakfast on the QT
intro: Finance Minister Mathias Cormann had an interesting breakfast date at the QT Hotel in Canberra on Thursday: none other than the Member for Fairfax, Clive Palmer.

headline: Lunch watch
intro: In Sydney on Thursday we spotted Built chairman Marco Rossi lunching with Morgan Stanley's investment banking chief, Richard Wagner, and his property specialist David Dixon.

headline: Albanese farewells Max the Axe
intro: Labor infrastructure spokesman Anthony Albanese is our early pick for 2016 Australian of the Year, for his O.U.T.S.T.A.N.D.I.N.G statement on Thursday responding to Sydney Airport chairman Max Moore-Wilton's stated intention to retire.

headline: Kids' hospital fundraiser
intro: Aussie John Symond will fling open the doors to his Point Piper mansion on Friday night for the 15th annual Silver Party. The event will raise at least $500,000 for the Sydney Children's Hospital's thoracic ward.

headline: Countplus in turnaround
intro: Millionaire Barry Lambert's $47 million listed accountancy group, Countplus, is in turnaround mode with new chief executive Phil Aris announcing a 20 per cent increase in underlying net profit for the six months to December 2015, once $2.4 million worth of non-recurring loyalty payments to Commonwealth Bank is excluded.

headline: Review takes shine off Money3
intro: Payday lender Money3 has more than doubled its net profit for the half as an acquisition streak continued and increased its full-year guidance despite looming regulatory scrutiny on the controversial sector.

headline: Cloud write-off casts $7m shadow on BoQ
intro: Bank of Queensland will take a $7 million hit to its half-year earnings after it announced regulators had blocked plans to introduce a new cloud-based customer relationship management system.

headline: MYOB hits back at rival Xero's big deal
intro: We are a profitable business that has very high cash generation MYOB chief executive Tim Reed (pictured)

headline: Treasury spends $1m on PR and surveys
intro: The government has spent more than $1 million on public relations, surveys, internet consultants - and developing "brand architecture" such as fonts - for the overdue tax white paper and intergenerational report.

headline: Tax white paper to look at super change proposals
intro: Treasurer Joe Hockey has raised the possibility of taking superannuation tax changes to the next election following a proposal by the Greens to apply a sliding scale to contributions.

headline: Dollar dives as weak capex fuels rate-cut bets
intro: The Australian dollar dropped by almost half a cent, as investors shortened the odds of a March rate cut after the release of weak capital expenditure data on Thursday.

headline: Oil Search makes strides
intro: Cheery news in today's world of low growth, oversupply and soft commodity prices is hard to find, but it is still out there.

headline: Price approaches six-year lows
intro: After trading slightly higher for the first session after the week-long Lunar New Year holiday, iron ore has slumped to a near six-year low amid a lack of demand from Chinese steel mills.

headline: Bank price bubble fear
intro: Australian bank share prices are heading for a "bigger bubble" as falling rates in the country and low global bond yields support a continued hunt for yield in Australia's equity market, Gerard Minack of Minack Advisors says.

headline: Euroz
intro: Perth-based broking and advisory firm Euroz swung to a loss in the six months ended December 31, as softer commodity prices weighed on the value of its stakes in Westoz Investment Company and Ozgrowth Limited.

headline: Tree values boost TFS
intro: Indian sandalwood producer TFS Corp has increased its full-year guidance, after posting a record half-year profit, boosted by revaluations of its plantations and a stronger US dollar.

headline: Foreign farm investors face lower thresholds
intro: There is a big change coming to how Australia's foreign investment laws apply to agricultural land. This change coincides with the increase in mergers and acquisitions in the food and agriculture sector generally.

headline: Brydon cements profit
intro: Adelaide Brighton boss Martin Brydon said he will pursue funding from the Abbott government's $2.55 billion Emissions Reduction Fund as the construction materials group accelerates alternative fuel use to head off its rising gas bill.

headline: Sandfire Resources
intro: Lower copper prices reduced Sandfire Resources' interim net profit by 9 per cent but chief financial officer Matthew Fitzgerald said the falling local currency has helped the Australian dollar copper price "claw back". The miner increased the volumes of both gold and copper sold, boosting sales revenue to $264.2 million. Mining was temporarily suspended at DeGrussa during November and December due to dewatering issues and as a result, ore production was below the targeted annualised rate for the period. Mr Fitzgerald said the company expects a stronger second half on the back of increased copper production and lower costs.

headline: Fantastic Holdings
intro: Discount furniture retailer Fantastic rewarded shareholders with a 4c-a-share special dividend and doubled its interim payout after net profit rebounded 43 per cent to $6.9 million in the December-half. Same-store sales growth accelerated in January and February but managing director Stephen Heath said the weaker $A could offset cost savings and gross margin gains in the second half.

headline: Macquarie Atlas Roads
intro: Macquarie Atlas Roads reported an annual net loss after paying a $58.2 million performance fee to managers Macquarie. The company said discussions were "ongoing" with the French government over its plans to renegotiate new toll fares on French roads, including Macquarie Atlas' key investment, the Autoroutes Paris-Rhin-Rhone. A new chairman, board director Nora Scheinkestel, will replace David Walsh in April.

headline: Japara Healthcare
intro: Japara Healthcare chief Andrew Sudholz says the newly listed aged-care operator is on track to meet the full-year earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation prospectus forecast of $50.3 million. After listing last April at $2.00, Japara got a major shock when the for-profit sector's payroll tax supplement was slashed last year. Mr Sudholz said this would strip $4 million from pre-tax earnings for 2014-15.

headline: Select Harvests
intro: Select Harvests expects to benefit from the weaker Australian dollar and high almond prices caused by supply concerns as the almond group reported a 17 per cent rise in underlying first half profit to $21.5 million. The company is an owner and manager of orchards, processes almonds, and supplies consumer brands including Lucky, Sunsol and Soland. Protracted drought in California, which produces 80 per cent of the world's almonds, has been threatening supply at a time when demand is growing strongly. "Our current projection is a crop 30 per cent larger than last year, with almond price up 20 per cent. We look forward to a trouble free harvest and taking advantage of the strong market conditions," Select Harvests' managing director Paul Thompson said.

headline: Big city motorists reap benefit of cheaper petrol while regions lag
intro: Australian motorists will save on average $1000 if petrol prices continue to fall at the rate they did in the past 12 months.

headline: PetroChina: costs derailed Arrow deal
intro: One of China's biggest investors in Australia has blamed overly strict regulations on compliance and environmental protection for derailing a $20 billion-plus liquefied natural gas project planned in Queensland.

headline: Foreign investment crackdown a 'shambles'
intro: The Abbott government's foreign investment crackdown looks shaky after Labor reserved judgment on whether it will support the plan, which includes tougher fees and penalties, some of which start on Monday without any draft law in sight.

headline: SAI Global boss has no fear of more takeover bids
intro: SAI Global, which publishes the standards and regulations all companies must comply with, is restructuring and cutting costs as fast as it can. It has too. Last year it evaded a $1.1 billion takeover bid and with the added impetus of the benefit of the dollar, its new chief executive Peter Mullins is determined to look forward, not backward.

headline: Sydney Airport chair calls it a day
intro: Sydney Airport is searching for a new chairman after long-serving Max Moore-Wilton announced plans to step down in May after another year of earnings growth at the airport operator.

headline: Vissla slips into surf shops
intro: While Billabong International continues to address a slide in sales in key regions, its former executives are focused on establishing their new brand, Vissla, in a crowded market.

headline: Billabong still has long wave to ride
intro: Surf, ski and skate-wear retailer Billabong International has begun phase two of an ambitious turnaround plan - building global omni-channel and supply chain platforms and rationalising its Australian stores - after stabilising its American and European operations and moving back into the black for the first time in three years.

headline: National Archives builds last paper store
intro: Some of the nation's most precious historic parchments, as well as more than 40 million Commonwealth records, will be housed in a new custom-built bunker in Canberra. It will be the last repository the National Archives of Australia builds for storing paper - future storage centres will be digital.

headline: Peet profits despite WA
intro: Developer Peet Ltd has shrugged off the slowing Western Australian housing market, saying the market remains solid and that prices are static.

headline: Aus Industrial rejects 360 bid
intro: The $225 million Australian Industrial REIT, managed by Fife Capital, has formally rejected a takeover bid by rival 360 Capital Industrial Fund, telling its shareholders the offer was not as attractive as their current investment.

headline: AMP on notice for Exchange Plaza
intro: Exchange Plaza in Perth's CBD could again hit the market this year after AMP was issued with a pre-emptive notice by the co-owner this month.

headline: Briefs
intro: Simonds hits profit targets

headline: Fyodor's flat
intro: Jeffrey Tayler hopes to be reinspired, despite Russian authoritarian gloom, and revisits some Dostoyevsky homes.

headline: Lego profits look like child's play
intro: Copenhagen | Metalbeard's Sea Cow, a Jungle Tree Sanctuary and Arctic Base Camp were among the products that propelled Lego to record sales and earnings in 2014, cementing its position as the world's most profitable toymaker.

headline: Petrobras downgrade rocks Brazil's markets
intro: Sao Paulo | Brazil's bonds, equities and currency were rocked yesterday after Moody's cut its rating of state-controlled oil company Petrobras to junk status, citing a corruption scandal at the group.

headline: Singapore must surpass its founder's legacy
intro: With the possible exception of Fidel Castro's Cuba, there are few nations that so closely reflect one man's legacy as Singapore.

headline: Foreign buyers hit by substantial fees
intro: Everyone agreed that the rules on foreign investors buying Australian residential property had to be enforced. And everyone acknowledged that a small fee was needed to cover the extra cost.

headline: Special report liftout: Online trading
intro: Online traders are flocking back to the sharemarket as the S&P/ASX 200 heads towards 6000. Much of the momentum is being attributed to the rising share and property markets as traders relish an increase in their household wealth. About 85,000 dormant traders - those who had not traded in the previous 12 months - returned to online trading in the second half of last year, according to researchers Investment Trends.

headline: New Treasury head fan of Reagan's 1980s tax cuts
intro: New Treasury secretary John Fraser has declared he has an "old fashioned" dislike of government debt, said using budget spending to spur economic growth doesn't work and lauded Ronald Reagan's 1980s tax cuts for reigniting American entrepreneurial spirits.

headline: Good news breathes fire into sharemarkets
intro: Sounding an upbeat note about the US economy, Federal Reserve chair Janet Yellen started preparing investors for an increase in US interest rates as early as June, a message of confidence that helped drive shares to highs around the world.

headline: Outrage over PM's property hit
intro: The federal government faces a backlash from the property sector over plans to charge foreign homebuyers a tax of up to 1 per cent to fund the scrutiny of purchases by the Foreign Investment Review Board.

headline: Melbourne to rule as Sydney remains flat
intro: Almost half of all new apartments built over the next five years will be in Melbourne, mainly because planning and other bottlenecks are holding up growth in Sydney.

headline: Home and apartment building hits record $54.4b in 2014
intro: Housing and apartment construction hit a record $54.4 billion last year, driven by a pre-Christmas boom.

headline: Dispute sees mall development slow
intro: Scentre Group has scaled back work on a shopping mall development on the Gold Coast, after an apparent dispute with the new state government over funding of a planned Pacific Motorway interchange necessary to create access to the site.

headline: Australians vote like Greeks on reform
intro: The leaders of Australia's biggest real estate groups say Australia is heading down the path of Greece because politicians trying to make tough decisions will keep being voted out.

headline: Appointments: Shipp on board at CBRE
intro: CBRE has appointed Brendan Shipp to its office services and metropolitan investment properties team in south Sydney.

headline: IOOF snares $22m Melbourne office
intro: ASX-listed IOOF Holdings has snapped up an office building in Melbourne's south-east for about $22 million as record amounts of capital turn to the suburbs for commercial real estate opportunities.

headline: It's business as usual for Investa Commercial fund
intro: The Investa Commercial Property Fund has accepted it cannot exercise pre-emptive rights over as much as $1 billion worth of real estate at this stage, but fund manager Peter Menegazzo said the uncertainty will not get in the way of business.

headline: Bidders queue up for Morgan Stanley sale
intro: At least 30 parties have expressed interest in the sale of Morgan Stanley's $8.9 billion Investa Office and land business in Australia, with the first round of bidders likely to be finalised in a matter of weeks.

headline: Victorian government acts quickly to please unions
intro: During its three months in power the new Victorian Labor government has implemented five policies that directly benefit unions, and is considering a law that would allow it to alter the scope of royal commissions, including the one on trade unions initiated by the federal government.

headline: JPMorgan lures Holsheimer
intro: Ryan Holsheimer has left Bank of America Merrill Lynch, as revealed by Street Talk Online on Wednesday.

headline: Venture capital firm seeks Australian backers
intro: California-based Finistere Ventures is in Australia speaking to potential backers and scouring the market for investment opportunities, after its first close of a new $US150 million ($190 million) venture capital fund.

headline: Seven unlikely to go high-voltage on Beach
intro: Seven Group has shed some light on its highly secretive listed investment portfolio and how it could feature as chief executive Don Voelte ramps up the company's oil and gas presence.

headline: Morgan Stanley steams ahead with Aurizon Holdings block
intro: The block games have begun.

headline: Youi insurance touted as IPO candidate
intro: Insurance floats were front and centre as the initial public offering market opened two years ago - and bankers are doing their best to make sure the sector's listing spree isn't over yet.

headline: Ruling could make life easier for construction companies
intro: The full Federal Court criticised the Fair Work Commission for insisting that unions be involved when workplace agreements are settled for new projects, in a decision that could make life easier for construction companies.

headline: Annual wage growth falls to 17-year low
intro: Annual wages growth has fallen to a 17-year low of 2.5 per cent, with private sector employees in Western Australia receiving yearly pay rises of just 2 per cent, illustrating the weakened resources sector.

headline: Federal, state cloud on NDIS
intro: A brawl has erupted between the federal government and the states over a federal move to turn over at least half the board that oversees the National Disability Insurance Scheme.

headline: Bush named to head turnaround
intro: Struggling radio and television network Southern Cross Austereo has persuaded its lenders to ease covenants and appointed corporate turnaround specialist Peter Bush as its new chairman in a bid to reassure investors.

headline: East Coast gas aids APA
intro: Gas transporter APA Group has tapped into increased opportunities to move gas around the grid with the start-up of LNG exports in Queensland, allowing it to raise its guidance for full-year net profit.

headline: Time for Virgin Australia to turn a profit: Air NZ
intro: Air New Zealand chief executive Christopher Luxon, who sits on the board of Virgin Australia Holdings, has declared it is time for the Australian carrier to "get profitable".

headline: Infigen Energy
intro: Wind power producer Infigen Energy climbed into the black in the first half, but managing director Miles George warned that uncertainty over the Renewable Energy Target (RET) legislation is damaging performance. The $1.6 million profit for the December half was up from a $16.9 million loss earlier, which included one-off charges. Production dropped 6 per cent to 2103 gigawatt-hours. Mr George said he was "pleased" with the result given poor wind conditions and electricity prices in Australia. He said the lack of clarity over the future of the RET was also eroding investor confidence in Australia.

headline: AWE
intro: AWE has dived to a $61.7 million first-half loss, mostly due to a $50.1 million asset write-down because of the drop in oil prices. Sales revenues slipped 8.1 per cent to $161.7 million on production of 2.6 million barrels of oil equivalent, in line with full-year guidance of 4.6 million to 5.1 million boe. Managing director Bruce Clement described the result as "solid" despite the hit from the plunge in prices and that AWE was continuing to expand. Citigroup analyst Dale Koenders said the loss was more severe than estimated, mostly due to higher than expected exploration expenses and depreciation and amortisation charges. Angela Macdonald-Smith

headline: Macmahon Holdings
intro: Macmahon Holdings is the latest mining services company to post a half-year loss as belt-tightening by the big miners leads to heavy write-downs.

headline: Helloworld
intro: Helloworld, the travel company part-owned by Qantas, narrowed its loss in the first half due largely to a reduction in the cost of attempting to turn around its poor financial performance. However, the company previously known as Jetset Travelworld has forecast a drop in pretax earnings this financial year due to weak consumer sentiment and it is continuing to pour money into boosting its presence online. It had a net loss of $736,000 for the six months to December, compared with a $4.7 million loss in the prior period. Revenue fell 8 per cent to $139 million, while operating costs dropped 3 per cent. Matt O'Sullivan

headline: ASIC used legal powers to extract NAB information
intro: The corporate regulator has used formal legal powers to gather more information from National Australia Bank, after it was revealed the bank paid $10 million to $15 million to customers who received inappropriate advice. Australian Securities and Investments Commission chairman Greg Medcraft said the watchdog has also entered into talks with NAB to review compensation of financial advice clients, and clamping down on bad advice remains a top priority.

headline: Former judge quits allegedly corrupt firm
intro: Former NSW Attorney General and Supreme Court Justice John Dowd has resigned as chairman of a construction company after the federal police charged his fellow directors with allegedly bribing Iraqi officials to win a multi-million dollar contact.

headline: Abbott to send 200 extra troops to Iraq in joint taskforce
intro: Australia is poised to deploy more than 200 extra troops to Iraq as part of a joint training taskforce with New Zealand to bolster the campaign against Islamist militants.

headline: Fringe festival
intro: Performers on stage during a media call for the production of the musical Sweet Charity, which earned three gongs at this year's Helpmann awards. The show opened at the Arts Centre in Melbourne yesterday.

headline: Baird aims to steal thunder as launches go head-to-head
intro: Premier Mike Baird's NSW Coalition party is attempting to crowd out the Labor Party's campaign launch this Sunday by holding a campaign rally on the same day in the battleground seat of Mirandra.

headline: States demand fair deal on infrastructure
intro: The states have demanded the Abbott government is fair about distributing rebates for asset sales if the proposed legislation for the asset recycling scheme fails to pass the Senate.

headline: Wilson flags write-down, cost cuts after spin-off
intro: Wilson HTM Investment Group has flagged cost-cutting and a possible accounting write-down that will follow the mooted spin-off of its securities unit, as the company posted an increase in interim profit.

headline: ClearView has the premium success recipe
intro: ClearView Wealth has posted a 9 per cent increase in underlying profits to $9.9 million for the half-year to December, reflecting steady growth in its life insurance business.

headline: Veda prudent despite regulatory advantages
intro: Data company Veda Group will benefit from a lengthening list of regulatory and market changes that require extensive identity checks, but has kept its low double digit earnings growth forecast for 2015.

headline: Macquarie offloads asset finance unit
intro: Macquarie Group has sold another business in its corporate asset finance unit, offloading Macquarie Equipment Finance in the United States to lender Huntington Bancshares as it continues to redeploy capital.

headline: Investment bank clients 'must lobby' for changes

International sales rose 45 per cent to $40.4 million due to strong demand for pokies sold in revenue sharing deals.

headline: Design

One in particular had a gold foil exterior and a dark ganache filling. As I cut the chocolate in half, the idea came to me.” The idea was for a suite of side tables, variously faceted and finished in a selection of luxurious materials and sexy textures. Using 3D modelling software, Farrell truncated some planes and dimpled others, creating nuanced sculptural modules that work by themselves or grouped. With polished bronze vertical surfaces and lush walnut tops, each piece is an enticement to the eye and the touch. Sweet.

headline: Sculpture

In Chess is a Sitting Sport the Vienna-based sculptor remodels the ubiquitous plastic stackable chair into a hierarchical chess set, with a stool representing the pawn and the queen given a crown-shaped back. Only the king is unmodified. “In a historical view of Western civilisation, the chair is a development of the throne. Only kings were allowed to rest,” says Loechner.

headline: Insert

His installations, some in parts of the prison usually off limits to the public, have been integrated into the site to great effect. In the old hospital wing, for example, the bathtubs, toilets and sinks are filled with white porcelain flowers, evoking among other things Mao Zedong’s “hundred flowers ” campaign. Another work features a series of carpets made up of Lego-style tiles which depict international prisoners of conscience, past and present. @Large: Ai Weiwei on Alcatraz runs until April 26.

headline: Too complex to be fair
intro: Fundamental to a fair system is one which is simply understood. In the editorial "Fair tax system can be improved" (AFR, February 20) you commented on the shadow treasurer's inability to recall the low income tax threshold or the tax rate. A more meaningful question for both the Treasurer and the shadow treasurer would be for them to explain in simple terms the calculation of the effective marginal tax rate (EMTR) for taxpayers, particularly those in families with children. The complexity of this question is obvious from the "comprehensive tax calculator" questionnaire provided on the ATO's website. An indicated 15 to 25 minutes is required to complete the questionnaire on the assumption taxable income is already known. The answer is also likely to be further complicated by the rate of withdrawal of other social security benefits resulting in high marginal rates. The high level of EMTRs and their complexity clearly need to be addressed to achieve a fair tax system.

headline: Drugs not the whole answer
intro: Professor Jon Jureidini's warning on the problems of applying a "disease model" to adolescent distress is welcome ("Experts split on the best way to help teens beat the blues", Men's Health, February 18). The problem with Patrick McGory's "early intervention" approach to adolescent angst is that the listening ear, provision of information and cognitive behaviour therapy gets short shrift once the patient enters the "mental health" system. In a world of the quick fix, the acceleration to prescription drugs as the answer to depression and anxiety is all too easy. Antidepressants, antipsychotics and insomnia medications, increasingly prescribed in unison, are often psychologically or physically addictive, produce serious physical and metabolic symptoms, especially over the long term, and, ironically, can increase anxiety. Ample research has shown that the difference in effectiveness between "mental health" drugs and a placebo can be slight but the damaging reactions produced by these powerful drugs are serious.The side effects of weight gain, lack of balance, cognitive decline/dulling of responses and neurological and metabolic damage are receiving little attention in the mainstream media. Time to start questioning whether psychiatric drug treatments place adolescents and adults, particularly the aged, on a treadmill to a list of health problems that in turn are treated with more drugs. The ever widening of the mental health net is all profit for the drug companies but should be a strong warning for consumers to ask far more questions, to thoroughly research the potential downside of medication with mind-altering drugs.

headline: Adam Giles Northern Territory
intro: Adam Giles is the Julia Gillard of Indigenous politics. Like Gillard he was hailed as a "first", the first ever Indigenous state or territory leader. But, also like Gillard, he took power in a palace coup in 2013, while the previous chief minister was on a trade mission to Japan, and has spent the past two years dealing with a divided and disloyal party. Just this month, his deputy briefly announced at 1am that Giles had been sacked by his caucus. But Giles fought back and is still there - just. His main national mission is to win federal cash for a pipeline to the south-east for Northern Territory gas and ensure Indigenous funding is not cut in any deal on commonwealth state relations. He has played down the importance of his Indigenous background and he himself hails from the Blue Mountains in NSW and not a remote community. But the issue of race is always around in the Northern Territory. He rose to power after masterminding a successful strategy of winning Indigenous voters over to the Country Liberals. But his leadership was shaken last year after two disgruntled Indigenous MPs defected to Clive Palmer.

headline: Jay Weatherill South Australia
intro: Jay Weatherill is big on people power and listening first. The quietly-spoken 50-year-old wants robust public debate about big picture changes he's tackling to transform the creaking South Australia economy. This include a 30-minute shift in time zone, entry into the nuclear industry and a radical shake-up of state taxes. There's also a steely resolve and ambition. He earned the nickname the "smiling assassin" for elbowing aside a long-serving sitting MP to win pre-selection for his western Adelaide suburbs seat in 1999 to enter politics, stepping out of a law practice. Weatherill, who is married to Melissa Bailey and has two young daughters, studied economics and law at Adelaide University. As a young man, he was in a relationship with uni student Penny Wong, who later became federal Finance Minister. He's from the left wing of the ALP and in Year 11 at the beachside Henley High School penned a poem displaying his strident opposition to nuclear energy. That's now changed. He's been in the top job since late 2011 and his skills as a persuasive negotiator helped convince factional bosses he was the right person to lead, as Mike Rann's popularity waned among voters. headline: Annastacia Palaszczuk Queensland
intro: People may not have been able to spell her name, let alone pronounce it correctly before the January's state election, but Annastacia Palaszczuk has burst onto the national stage since the shock defeat of the Newman Liberal National Party government. Although she was a minister in the former Bligh government, Palaszczuk has flown below the radar as state opposition leader for the past three years, namely because nobody expected the Campbell Newman - with the largest parliamentary majority in Australia - to lose the unloseable election. The 45-year-old Palaszczuk (pronounced Pala-shay) is the daughter of popular former Beattie government minister Henry Palaszczuk. She has been married twice before, including to former journalist from The Australian George Megalogenis. The trained lawyer, with a Masters in Arts from the London School of Economics, was just about to embark on life as solicitor when her father's western Brisbane seat of Inala became vacant in 2006. She says creating jobs is her main priority - the state's unemployment rate is now 6.5 per cent - but there's no big infrastructure projects to kickstart the economy. She's won the election, now the hard part begins. MARK LUDLOW

headline: Andrew Barr ACT
intro: Andrew Barr is heir apparent to Katy Gallagher, who stepped down from the role of Chief Minister to take up the lucrative offer of a safe federal Senate seat in December 2014. Barr is the first openly gay leader of a state or territory in Australia. He is a rarity within ACT Labor politics, being a member of the right wing of the party. He may have only been in the top job for less than three months, but Barr's experience as the longest-serving Treasurer in Australian politics gives some clue as to his policy bent. In that role he oversaw some of the most ambitious taxation reform in the country, phasing out inefficient transaction taxes like stamp duty and increasing the territory's reliance on land-based taxes. The Territory is, in fact, the only jurisdiction to have acted upon many of the recommendations of the 2010 national taxation review undertaken by Ken Henry. He has also borne the brunt of an unpopular rise in council duties, which have earned him never-ending grumbles from Canberrans. His agenda as Chief Minister includes a focus on infrastructure, having inherited from Gallagher a major light rail project designed to link satellite suburbs with the Canberra CBD, expected to cost at least $614 million. headline: Will Hodgman Tasmania
intro: Will Hodgman is continuing a family business. Except for two years since 1955 there has been a Hodgman in either Tasmania's Legislative Council or House of Assembly. Hodgman's own father, the late Michael Hodgman, was a member for the federal seat of Denison during the Malcolm Fraser government. He later served in Tasmania's lower house alongside his son. But where the old man was colourful - he was known in Canberra as the "mouth from the south" - the son is relatively low-key. Hodgman, who was born in 1969, is a new generation - if not new-age - politician married to an Englishwoman whom he met while working in London after graduating in law and arts from the University of Tasmania. He is a Republican who describes himself as a moderate. In his maiden speech as a newly elected MP to the House of Assembly back in 2002 he observed that Tasmania's Parliament featured a "new breed, a new generation of parliamentarians". Hodgman became Deputy Leader of the Opposition on election. It took him 12 years and one disappointing election result as Leader of the Opposition to become Premier. The family business continues.

headline: Colin Barnett Western Australia
intro: A staunchly proud West Australian, Colin Barnett has long been a thorn in the side of federal politicians. A strong defender of state rights, Barnett was the only premier not to sign the Rudd government's health reforms until it was unshackled from GST revenue, and refused to sign the Gonski reforms. His strong and at times minority view on issues such as remerging the state's energy assets has earned him the derogatory moniker The Emperor. The straight talking father of four, who famously lived without air-conditioning until promising wife Lyn he would install it if he won the 2013 election, believes he has been dealt a once-in-a-generation opportunity to transform Western Australia. He has spent the vast bounty of the resources boom on building hospitals, a sports stadium, redeveloping the waterfront and overhauling the city centre. Criticised for losing the state's triple A credit rating and pushing debt to $22 billion, Barnett believes future generations will appreciate the overhaul. A frustrated footballer who played for the Claremont Tigers as a teenager, Barnett, 64, was planning to retire before becoming Liberal opposition leader in 2008 one day before Labor's Alan Carpenter called a surprise election. headline: Daniel Andrews Victoria
intro: Daniel Andrews put it about before the November poll that saw Labor consign the Coalition to opposition after one term that he would prefer to be called folksy "Dan". The name didn't stick to the former Labor organiser, assistant state secretary, minister in the Brumby government and member of Labor's Socialist Left faction. Dan - or Daniel - Andrews has known little else but politics since graduating from Monash University in 1996 after spending part of his youth in Wangaratta, where he attended Marist Brothers' Galen College. He was born in Williamstown (like Clive Palmer) on July 6, 1972, just a few months before the Gough Whitlam Labor government was elected. The Andrews family are battlers who have run small businesses over the years. Andrews is described as a "devout" Catholic, but is at odds with the church on issues like gay marriage and abortion rights. He is regarded as bookish and a bit of a nerd, but if he has one passion - apart from politics - it is golf. He is a useful player, having once got his handicap down to six. It has now gone out to 10. Given the challenges as premier, including Victoria's infrastructure mess, he won't have much time to spend on the golf course. TONY WALKER

headline: Mike Baird New South Wales
intro: Mike Baird is the poster boy of Australian politics. The NSW Premier is feted in Sydney's boardrooms. Smitten young fans rush the Manly surfer for selfies. Even Baird's political opponents concede the ex-banker's talents - even if they won't put their name to it publicly. "He's a really good guy. It's horrible," one of the most senior members of NSW Labor told AFR Weekend in mock disgust. The son of a politician, Baird resisted the family trade. First he went into banking - at NAB, then Deutsche, then HSBC. Last April, seven years after Baird entered the NSW parliament, he was elevated from Treasurer to Premier following a Penfolds Grange-related brain snap by his predecessor Barry O'Farrell. His campaign pitch for the March 28 election is to privatise 49 per cent of the state's "poles and wires" electricity businesses to fund $20 billion of much-needed rails, roads and tunnels. If Baird can do what Campbell Newman failed to do - as opinion polls suggest he will - it will be a sharp rejoinder to claims that economic reform has become impossible in contemporary Australia. It seems that with good leadership, things can happen. Surely not long for the "Baird for Canberra" push to begin. WILL GLASGOW

But any shortage of gas for the massive processing "trains" on the three Curtis Island projects would intensify the crunch from falling world oil prices, which ultimately set internationally traded gas prices. And it would underline concerns that Australia has missed a major opportunity to develop its gas reserves when oil prices were high, in part due to repeated failure by state and federal governments to forge any overall energy sector strategy in the face of environmental zealots and farmers blocking exploitation of reserves on the basis of mostly trumped-up scare campaigns.

headline: Equitable representation enhances social cohesion
intro: We've all grown up thinking that the way we do democracy today is the best on offer. So famously said Winston Churchill. We groom charismatic and articulate political performers whose primary skill is to debate, divide and conquer. In the development of public policy, we all value the contest of ideas, but only if it leads to effective government, which usually requires tradeoffs. Today, in the absence of real ideological positions, candidates, parties (and their respective constituencies) tend to manufacture their differences. Rather than facilitating public understanding and common ground over difficult public policy issues, elections have morphed into tribal, sloganeering contests. In this political landscape, our parliaments are incapable of doing what they're designed to do: encourage deliberation and collaboration.

headline: MP super still generous
intro: David Leyonhjelm's opinion piece ("Pensions are for the poor alone", AFR, February 13) contains the following exculpatory statement that cannot go without comment. "Finally, before anyone complains about hypocrisy from a politician, I should point out that the scheme giving retired federal politicians a generous life pension was closed in 2004. New politicians like me contribute to a superannuation fund, the same as everyone else who has a job. And, like everyone else, whether we will need welfare in the form of a pension depends on how much super we manage to save, not how much or how long we have paid tax." Under the 2004 parliamentary scheme the government contributes 15.4 per cent of parliamentary salary, including allowances. If Leyonhjelm gets two Senate terms, the effect of the higher contribution rate over a flat 9.5 per cent contribution rate is a factor of about 1.6. His statement that he contributes to a fund "the same as everyone" should be judged in that context.

headline: Train MPs in public trust

Some Australian parliaments do provide comprehensive induction programs. Queensland became a leader after Tony Fitzgerald's inquiry revealed that not even a former premier understood the fundamentals of Australia's parliamentary system properly. The five-day induction program for Queensland's new state MPs is among the world's best. It is spaced out over several weeks, uses experiential learning techniques and covers issues that are fundamental to a parliamentary system of government.

headline: Budget failure will reverse fortune

Australia's economic structure as a capital-importing commodity exporter means we have more typically been hit relatively hard by global troubles, such as in the 1890s, the 1930s and the early 1980s. headline: Why China could avoid hard landing
intro: New York | Timothy Geithner admits no other country has ever successfully pulled off the kind of economic transition China is attempting. Yet the former US Treasury Secretary says he has a ‘‘lot of confidence’’ China’s leadership has learnt from past mistakes overseas and can avoid a hard landing. Mr Geithner, a key architect of the US government’s response to the 2008 financial crisis, gave three key reasons why he was optimistic about the economic and financial outlook for China, in rare public comments in New York. First, China has high rates of savings, he said. Second, although the China boom in recent years has been funded by large amounts of debt, Mr Geithner said it was financed largely out of local currency. Hence, this removes the risk of a currency crisis that pulled down Asian emerging market economies in the late 1990s. Third, unlike the modern capitalist economies such as the United States, the financial system in China is still overwhelmingly run by and guaranteed by the government. Mr Geithner, a former president of the New York Federal Reserve, said there were inefficiencies in state controlled banking. However, the public sector backing essentially removed the risks of ‘‘runs and panics’’ that afflicted Western banking systems in 2008. ‘‘If you look at what they’ve done in these last 18 months or so to try to mitigate the acute risks of this huge boom in financing … they’ve been very adept and very careful,’’ Mr Geithner said at The Economist magazine’s Buttonwood Gathering on Tuesday. ‘‘I have a lot of confidence in the people who have the economic reins. They’re very talented people and they have the benefit of watching the mistakes countries around the world made.’’ His views may provide comfort to Australian businesses and policymakers. China is Australia’s largest trading partner and has recently recorded a run of disappointing economic data, raising questions about its economic durability and financial stability. China is trying to shift its economy from being dependent on investment in physical infrastructure and exports, to be propelled more by domestic consumption. Mr Geithner was the keynote speaker at the annual event, drawing together top economic officials, Wall Street financiers and geopolitical experts to debate the world economy. A key question raised was whether the recovering US could be the world’s ‘‘consumer of last resort’’ in the next few years, as the rest of the world struggles. ‘‘If your economic plan is to rely on United States’ consumption, you could be at risk,’’ said chairman of the White House Council of Economic Advisers, Jason Furman. Mr Geithner, now president of Wall Street private equity firm Warburg Pincus, warned the world economy was in a ‘‘messy and dark’’ place. What worries him most is that ‘‘weak’’ political institutions and central banks no longer have the fire power or capacity to respond to shocks, given interest rates are at or below zero in Europe and Japan. ‘‘We have a different kind of risk which is a world that – for large parts of the economy – has less room to adjust policy in response to more modest shocks,’’ he said. Those views are informed by his tenure serving as treasury secretary and New York Federal Reserve chief during the financial crisis. He admitted to being ‘‘scarred’’ by staring over the abyss in 2008 when Lehman Brothers collapsed and the US government was forced to bail out Wall Street. Today, Mr Geithner said the US economy was facing better challenges than any other major country in the world. ‘‘Our economy is in a stronger position today than it was in the decade before the crisis,’’ he said. ‘‘Much of what was good about the economy was artificial. Fundamentally, it’s a better economy today.’’ International Monetary Fund chief economist Olivier Blanchard said he was less pessimistic on the global economy due to lower oil prices.

In this day and age, we should at least have the option of online voting. Online voting has enormous advantages, including the ability to vote from anywhere (reducing the need for postal and absentee voting), the opportunity to prevent informal votes (and avoid debates on the validity of a ballot paper), instantaneous accurate counting of votes and large cost savings in printing, staffing and logistics. It's time for the AEC to make a genuine move into the 21st century.

headline: Asset sales no quick fix
intro: The Queensland government, like our national government, wants to lease, or sell, national assets. If the asset is returning a profit and employing Australians, both state and federal governments benefit. Queensland gets the revenue and Canberra saves on unemployment. Leasing is nothing more than a limited agreed term of sale for which the lessee becomes the rightful owner for an agreed period.The buyer or lessee, if paying the same or better for that asset, must reduce costs or increase revenue to produce a profit. If it grows revenue, it confirms the government is operating the asset inefficiently. If it is unable to increase revenue it will cut staff. Therefore the state governments may lease or sell at cost neutral but the federal government finances the unemployed. Governments must be sure assets are used efficiently and employing Australians on fair terms and conditions.

headline: Hit avoiders not patients

Australians need to be aware that even if the minister concedes to a 50¢ co-payment, this becomes law and can then be increased to $7 or better. Governments continuously advise us to "get off welfare, take any job". Those giving such advice need to practise what they preach. This can be achieved by introducing additional income streams. One such scheme exists - the growing area of legal tax avoidance schemes. Stop attempting to get blood from stones by punishing those that have little or nothing when an alternative exists. Remove these compounding tax avoidance schemes before they achieve what they did for Greece, Italy, the US and others - namely a universal financial collapse. What political party will display the courage to face this dilemma before it becomes a recession or at worst a catastrophe?

headline: Why Abbott has failed

After the 2010 federal election, which he technically won, Abbott soon insulted and alienated the independent MPs (particularly those who were former Coalition members). This was in contrast to the negotiating abilities of Julia Gillard, from which an informal coalition emerged that was untidy but achieved substantial legislation during its tenuous life. Even after his greater House of Reps victory three years later, Abbott showed no signs of real humility either to the Parliament nor his own party, with his successive (and foolish) "captain's picks"; adding to the obstacles self-placed in the way of his aims. These future political histories will note his competitive alpha male persona worked well in opposition but failed him and his party in government, to which he was simply unable to adapt.

headline: Laffer needs a fix

Punitive tax rules and constantly changing goalposts kill the drive to produce goods and services. The late and great Lee Kuan Yew showed how a tiny city state, with only the resources of well-directed human endeavour, could compete with the world. Such leadership in our resource-rich but over-regulated, over-taxed country could transform Australia.

headline: Physician, heal thyself
