This GP role needs to extend beyond providing advice to patients about "personal health apps". It needs GPs to reclaim their role as the primary healthcare professional managing their patient's healthcare, while helping them avoid future problems. Their current defensive role, referring patients for expensive tests and specialists is the starting point for much of the "technical inefficiency" in our health system. We need to look at paying GPs to manage the overall care of the patient. If helping their patients with apps and battling inaccuracies by Dr Google are part of that - well and good. But we also need to ask GPs to get a lot more active in other ways. And then pay them accordingly.

headline: ASIC not redefining the idea of association

Indeed, one of ASIC's goals is to encourage investors engaging collectively to pursue good corporate governance. Compliance issues under the takeover and substantial holding provisions may arise when investors take collective action in relation to an entity. ASIC is consulting on this issue and welcomes all views, but wants to correct misconceptions regarding the intended effect of our proposed updated guidance. While in some instances it can be clear whether conduct falls within or outside the scope of the law, due to the nature of concepts such as "relevant agreement" and "associate", there can be uncertainty regarding their application to a range of conduct. Potential ASIC action over misconduct will depend on whether it appears conduct undermines takeover and substantial shareholding disclosure laws, rather than simply for promoting good corporate governance. ASIC's proposed guidance is simply aimed at helping people understand their existing legal obligations.

The name change will require the approval of at least 75 per cent of votes cast by eligible shareholders. Leighton’s board, which is chaired by its chief executive Marcelino Ferna´ndez Verdes, has already approved the name change. Leighton has also filed an application to trademark ‘‘Pacific Construction Contractors’’ and ‘‘PCC’’ but has not revealed its plans for that name. Leighton continues to be haunted by corruption allegations as the federal police and the Australian Securities and Investments Commission investigate former Leighton executives over the company’s dealings between 2009 and 2011.

headline: Lessons in UK’s grocery fight
intro: An element of class and occasional snobbery dictates supermarket shopping in Britain. Satirical Facebook pages ‘‘Overheard in Waitrose’’ and ‘‘Overheard in Lidl’’ mock the contrasting customer bases of the nation’s poshest and cheapest grocers of choice. There was even a middle-class backlash this year against Waitrose’s decision to give customers free tea and coffee –a promotion scrapped after well-heeled shoppers were miffed as the masses piled in for hot beverages. The offer was part of a savage price war sweeping Britain’s supermarket industry, which has been seriously wounded over the past year. The rise of discount German grocers Aldi and Lidl, and a shift towards no-frills products, has hurt the once-powerful incumbents Tesco, Asda, Sainsbury’s and Morrisons. The UK supermarket industry has long been a model for Australia, and analysts in Britain say while the two markets have different characteristics, the Woolworths and Coles duopoly should ignore what it happening in Europe at their peril. Woolworths, like Tesco, is trying to invest back in service while keeping prices competitive. Coles is intent on driving prices down further. Aldi is growing fast, mainly at the expense of the Metcash-powered IGA chain, but has the big two in its sights. ‘‘Aldi clearly sees Australia as an opportunity. It’s not necessarily because Australia has fat margins, but the duopoly provides opportunities for new entrants,’’ Clive Black of Shore Capital Stockbrokers, one of Britain’s most prominent retail analysts, told The Australian Financial Review. ‘‘Coles and Woolworths could misjudge, and underestimate Aldi at their peril. It has a Germanic trait that is very structural and strong. It can take a generation view on the market. They [Aldi and Lidl] are well capitalised and very well run, with lost cost bases and an entrepreneurial culture.’’ There were early signs in Britain this week the incumbents are fighting back. Tesco, wounded by an ill-fated global expansion strategy and an accounting scandal, reports a resurgence in sales over the past 12 weeks. J Sainsbury this week posted its fifth consecutive quarter of declines. It says there is evidence of turning a corner, but food price deflation will persist for the year. Still, the sacrifice chains such as Tesco have made to fund savage price cuts is obvious as you walk into one of the hundreds of supermarkets around London. The inner-city convenience stores are shabby and all transactions are done at self-service check-outs. ‘‘Tesco became a shopper’s champion for so long, and in its aspiration to go global, it lost its core market. It is now trying to recapture that,’’ Black says. It won’t be an easy job and British analysts say the retail landscape has shifted permanently in Britain. While it was the financial crisis in 2009 – which originally prompted consumers to switch to discount groceries – which underpinned Aldi and Lidl’s rise in the UK, lower commodity prices and stiff competition sparked a price war late last year. ‘‘Those big four retailers, broadly as a group, have been losing market share since 2009. That is fine if you are growing. But what happened in the last year is you have seen prices start to fall,’’ consumer research firm Kantar’s head of retail, Fraser McKevitt, told the FinancialReview. ‘‘People are shopping around more and are less loyal. If you look at the demographic of people shopping in Aldi now they are pretty mass market. The discounters are no longer just for people who don’t have money.’’ Kantar’s latest market share figures haveTescoat28per cent,Asda at17per cent, Sainsbury’s at 16.8 per cent and Morrisons on 11 per cent. Lidl has a 3.5 per cent share. A spokeswoman for Lidl, with 620 stores in Britain, told the Financial Review there were no plans to open in Australia. Aldi, which arrived in 2001 and has 10 per cent of the Australian market, is expanding. Coles and Woolworths say the British model spoils shoppers for choice, and will not be replicated in Australia. But the key lesson remains. ‘‘The price of complacency has been massive. The big four have been sleeping at the wheel,’’ Black says. Michael Smith spent two weeks in Britain as a guest of the UK High Commission and British Airways.

Before mains landed, the pair had equity partners of the newly formed PwC-KPMG super power Greco-Roman wrestling for the best car parking space. The only steadfast law in this new empire was a prohibition on moustaches. "Ah," sighed Riddell. "Reminds me of my good old days at Touche Tohmatsu." On stage, oblivious to the wheeling and dealing on table 13, McInnes Wilson lawyer Mark Woolley, Nous Group consultant Zac Ashkanasy, and Accru accountant Graeme Jennings were plotting how to negotiate a pay rise, having just claimed the gong for advisers with the biggest client fan base. Ashkanasy conceded his chances of convincing mysterious Nous patriarch and Richard Branson lookalike "Timmy" to his way of thinking were slim. Back in Perth the next morning, sitting in an office overrun by helium balloons, Accru bean counter Graeme Jennings was reassuring his 84-year-old father - a former managing partner of Ernst & Young Perth - that this accolade didn't make Jennings jnr a bigger star than his dad. "He's contemplating a comeback just to have another crack at the title," said Jennings. PPB Advisory, having claimed the award for best accounting firm with revenue between $50 million and $500 million for three years out of the last six, thought now would be a foolish time to break with tradition. "We must be doing something right," PPB boss Stephen Purcell told his troops at a celebratory morning tea in Melbourne the following day. The tax nerds at Greenwoods & Herbert Smith Freehills carried off the award for best accounting firm revenue under $50 million. "Our clients have spoken. We're awesome," managing director Tony Frost told staff in a communique. Although, by Frost's own admission, "a few years ago, we won six [awards]".

David Murray's position of neutral gearing is consistent with this interpretation of the Tax Act.

headline: Densification a disaster
intro: That nine million homes are needed over the next 40 years is not in dispute ("Another nine million homes needed by 2055", AFR, March 6). The big question is where these nine million homes will be built - in existing suburbs or on the urban fringe? Urban densification is an idea that has failed all over the world. Whether it's traffic congestion, air pollution, the destruction of bio-diversity or the unsustainable pressure on electricity, water, sewage and stormwater infrastructure, urban densification has been a disaster. It is not good for the environment, it does not lead to a reduction in motor vehicle use, it does not save water, it does not result in nicer neighbourhoods, it does not stem the loss of agricultural land, it does not save on infrastructure costs for government and, worst of all, it puts home ownership out of the reach of those on low and middle incomes. By any measure low-density housing on the urban fringe leaves urban densification for dead.

Any tax review must consider the cost to the public of the revenue concessions for the NFP sector including GST, payroll tax, land tax and municipal rate concessions. We need to know the cost before deciding whether we can afford support. NFPs compete with businesses that do not enjoy these concessions. Who pockets the tax concessions?

headline: Super tax clarified
intro: The article "IGR will show us robbing the young to give to the old" (AFR, March 4) says, "In 2007 the Howard government made superannuation earnings tax-free for people over 60, as long as the account-holder is making some withdrawals. Superannuation accounts held by under-60s, by contrast, pay 15 per cent tax on all income." Both sentences are wrong. Fund earnings in pension phase remained exempt when taxation of fund income was introduced in 1988, and have remained so irrespective of the age of the pensioner. A change made in 2007 was to the taxation of pension payments for those over 60 years of age. These rules were made more generous, with no tax on most payments. It follows that if these rules are changed, it will affect many retirees, irrespective of the size of their pension.

We respect the sovereign status of Indonesia but are opposed to the death sentence. And given the remarkable rehabilitation of the two condemned men it would be wrong to execute them, even if one does not object to death sentences. It is important that Australia speaks with one voice, and that does include the business community. Sometimes it is important to put principle before profit.

headline: Ignoring natural limits

There are biophysical limits to the sustainable use of natural capital, and when these are exceeded the result is long-term land and water degradation and the permanent loss of biological diversity. Every state-of-the-environment report lists the scale of these issues, and that is why controls on clearing land and extraction of water resources are fundamental to, not a constraint on, a sustainable economy. We are not going to benefit from the world's growing food demand by degrading more land and draining more river systems. The future for Australian agriculture is the better use of science, innovation and markets to improve the efficiency of production without degrading natural capital.

headline: How we got the boom wrong
intro: As the Abbott government was retreating from its attempts to curb the inexorable growth of budget spending on subsidised health services on Tuesday, some were digesting an ominous idea from the Business Council of Australia's pre-budget submission. That the economy's terms of trade - the price we get for our exports compared the price we pay for our imports - will fall to closer to their historical average than predicted after soaring to their highest level on record back to at least 1870. This would mean that the export-based national income surge of the past decade's resources boom will retreat more than predicted. That would leave a bigger gap between what voters expect government to deliver and how much they are prepared to be taxed. More of the resource bounty than we thought was temporary and will not be available to fund the political promises - tax cuts but, more importantly, big rises in social spending - that governments have entered into. This fiscal gap goes to the heart of Canberra's political crisis: the inability to collectively agree that the biggest national income boost since the 1850s goldrush was largely a one-off that should have been invested or saved rather than consumed.

headline: Turnbull wise not to challenge yet

And this is perhaps 18 months before the next poll, when Mr Shorten is yet to be seriously tested on what alternative an unreconstructed Labor party would offer. headline: Triggs caught out

When the Abbott government came into office, the first thing it wanted to do was clean up Labor's disorganised mess, stem illegal boat arrivals and get children out of detention as soon as possible. headline: Recruitment results speak for themselves
intro: I refer to the article "Headhunters slammed over conflicts" (AFR, April 28). It is an eye-catching headline but I am sure your readers recognise when someone is 'talking their own book'. Rather than "neglecting proper due diligence" and "focusing … on placement fees", my experience is that the profession is very focused on getting its clients the very best result. Like many companies we follow up with our clients and successful candidates. Our most recent follow-up, in December 2014, recorded 86 per cent of our successful candidates in place two years after being appointed. I accept that means 14 per cent were no longer there but that is a far cry from Mind Group's assertion of 20-60 per cent turnover in 18 months.

headline: Don't double taxes
intro: Dividend imputation removed the inequitable double taxation of dividends ("Imputation calculation 'questionable"', AFR, April 28). If Joe Hockey's tax discussion paper considers this a "significant cost to revenue", what must he think of the "cost to revenue" of not doubling or tripling other taxes? Imagine the huge "costs to revenue" of taxpayers dying prematurely. Many investors rely on dividend imputation to fund their retirement, either directly or through managed funds. Any reversal of imputation would substantially reduce their income and send the shares of honest, tax-paying local companies into a capital tailspin. With anti-capital policies like this from the Liberals, there will be little left for the Greens.

headline: Longevity pooled options
intro: As Christopher Joye pointed out in "Why you're likely to outlast your nest egg" (AFR, April 24), there is a real chance many Australians will run out of money in retirement. What the article failed to reveal was that there are options that will ensure your super nest egg lasts as long you do. Joye suggests there are just two solutions: 1, put more money into super; or 2, accept a much lower standard of living in retirement. A better approach is a longevity pooling product. That is, those who die earlier leave some money for those who live longer. All retirees need flexibility and access to some capital, so it's feasible to consider investing a quarter of retirement benefits into a pooled product. Longevity pooled options are mutual products, require no capital, and have no shareholders. After expenses, all the capital and investment earnings are shared with the survivors.

headline: No proof that rule helps
intro: In his interview ("Courts, business up to the challenge", AFR, April 17) competition policy review panel member Michael O'Bryan, SC, defends the panel's recommended changes to Section 46 relating to the misuse of market power. He asserts that business is up to the task of answering: "Is this conduct directed to promoting or stymieing competition?" Pro-competitive aggressive pricing can have substantially lessen competition by reducing the number of competitors in a market. How can business know in advance what the effect will be of its competitive behaviour? The panel accepts its proposal carries the risk of deterring pro-competitive behaviour but claims the costs outweigh the benefits - without ever specifying or seeking to quantify those benefits.

headline: Roskam misses the point
intro: John Roskam ("Keeping to the law is fair in tax", AFR, April 17) suggests "there are so many things wrong about the current tax debate it's difficult to know where to start". Strange - I found myself thinking the same about his article. First, he contends that Australia is not a low taxing country only after "compulsory superannuation ... counted as taxes". Clearly they are not taxes. Second, that because there is a flat tax of 15 per cent on super contributions it is fair to all. This flies in the face of the generally accepted view that progressive tax systems are appropriate because the marginal utility, that is value in the hands of the holder, of the millionth dollar is dramatically lower than the first dollar. Third, that multinationals should only comply with the law and no more. Of course that's correct. However, if there is a policy view that the world has changed and the law needs to change to catch up, that's an entirely reasonable outcome to lobby for.
